exam: A patient with severe malaria presents with a pH 7.28, PaCO2 30 mmHg, HCO3‑ 15 mmol/L – what is the primary disorder and next step? — Identify metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation; start IV fluids, correct electrolytes, consider bicarbonate only if pH <7.1.

You receive a serum K+ of 6.8 mmol/L and peaked T waves on ECG – what immediate measures and why? — Give calcium gluconate to stabilise membranes, then insulin‑glucose and consider sodium bicarbonate; prevents ventricular arrhythmia.
A patient on diuretics has Na+ 124 mmol/L, urine Na+ 30 mmol/L – what type of hyponatraemia and management? — Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia; replace with isotonic saline, monitor Na+ rise.
How does an elevated anion gap guide you in a septic patient? — Suggests accumulation of lactate, ketoacids or toxins; look for sepsis, diabetic ketoacidosis, renal failure; treat underlying cause.

When is bicarbonate therapy contraindicated in metabolic acidosis? — In lactic acidosis from sepsis where it may increase CO2 load, or in patients with hypernatremia; avoid unless pH <7.1 or severe hyperkalaemia.
Explain why serum potassium may appear low in a patient with severe hyperlipidaemia. — Pseudohyponatraemia from indirect ISE; true K+ may be normal; confirm with direct ISE or plasma sample.

A child with sickle cell disease presents with abdominal pain, normal amylase, and a serum bicarbonate of 10 mmol/L – what is the likely cause? — Acute vaso‑occlusive crisis causing metabolic acidosis; treat pain, hydration, and monitor for infection.
What compensatory respiratory change occurs in chronic metabolic alkalosis? — Hypoventilation with elevated PaCO2 to retain CO2 and lower pH.
